clue.text: Utterance of first syllables on weak stomach?

indicators.note: only the opening syllable of each of the two words is kept, so their second syllables fall away

parts.note: a dicky heart or stomach is a weak or unreliable one, in British slang
tummy is the homely word for stomach

explanation.surface: A question about what someone stammers out when their gut is feeling fragile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weak stomach' is the British slang phrase 'dicky tummy'; only the first syllable of each word survives. 'On' is just a link: the first word sits on the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A dictum is a formal pronouncement or saying, so it is a kind of utterance.

clue.text: Put out a noise in a Corfu location

indicators.note: to put something out is to throw it into disorder, so the words that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone making a racket somewhere on the Greek island of Corfu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' tells you to rearrange the letters of A NOISE IN A.
explanation.definitionFit: Corfu is an island lying in that stretch of the Mediterranean west of Greece, so the sea is where it is located.

clue.text: Writer after circulation welcoming English or American one

indicators.note: welcoming means taking a guest inside, so one letter goes into the middle of the others
once the word has been passed around and shaken up its letters come out in a new order

parts.note: an author is a writer

explanation.surface: An author whose books have been in circulation, gaining English or American readers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After circulation' rearranges AUTHOR (the writer) to THORAU, and 'welcoming' puts E inside it. The definition is 'American one', meaning an American writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry David Thoreau, author of Walden, was a nineteenth-century writer from Massachusetts.

clue.text: Marks good Valley officer got in state educational institution

parts.note: M is an abbreviation for marks, the old German currency

indicators.note: the officer and the rest get in, meaning they are placed inside the word for state

parts.note: to allege is to state or assert
a dale is a valley, especially in northern England
NCO stands for non-commissioned officer

explanation.surface: A tale of grades, a valley and an army officer getting into some state school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got in' puts good, valley and officer inside the word for state, with M in front. Magdalen is pronounced 'maudlin'.
explanation.definitionFit: Magdalen is one of the constituent colleges of Oxford University, a place of learning.

clue.text: Quickly move home and its contents which may come with an Indian

definitions.text: which may come with an Indian

parts.note: to pop is to go somewhere quickly, as in popping out
a pad is slang for one's home or flat

indicators.note: the contents of a word are its inside letters, leaving out the first and last

explanation.surface: Advice to dash house with everything inside it, as a removals firm might put it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home' works twice: as PAD, and 'its contents' are the middle letters of 'home' itself, OM. 'An Indian' is British slang for a meal at an Indian restaurant.
explanation.definitionFit: This thin crisp lentil wafer is commonly served as a starter with a curry in Britain.

clue.text: Conspicuously good second of films about aquatic life

parts.note: pi is slang for pious, showily or ostentatiously virtuous
cine relates to cinema and films, as in cine camera

explanation.surface: Praise for a fine second feature among documentaries on underwater life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second of films' reads as the second letter of 'films', but 'second' gives S on its own and 'films' gives CINE.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things relating to fish, so it means concerning creatures of the water.

clue.text: Bungle's usual way to use a sock

definitions.meaning: to make a tactless blunder or gaffe

definitions.text: usual way to use a sock
definitions.meaning: a sock is normally worn by inserting the foot into it

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to say something embarrassingly tactless, a blunder; taken literally it describes pulling on hosiery.

clue.text: Possible Paralympian needing a bit of current united support

parts.note: the amp is the unit of electric current
a tee supports a golf ball before it is struck

explanation.surface: An athlete in disabled sport depending on a little electricity and a joint support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of current' is the unit AMP, not an extraction from the word 'current'.
explanation.definitionFit: Many competitors at the Paralympic Games have lost a limb, so such an athlete might be one.

clue.text: Ring tolerated deposing leader, like some old cabinets

parts.note: O is shaped like a ring

indicators.note: a leader deposed is removed from the head, so the word loses its first letter

parts.note: taken, as in 'taken in good part', can mean accepted or tolerated

explanation.surface: A ring kept despite a leader being ousted, as old governmental cabinets might do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deposing leader' removes T, the first letter of TAKEN. 'Cabinets' looks political but means furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: Traditional furniture was often made from solid oak wood, so such cupboards are oak-built.

clue.text: Fills printing space with Simenon, maybe dropping earlier European

parts.note: an en is a unit of width in printing

indicators.note: only the first of two identical letters in the name is dropped, the earlier one

parts.note: Georges Simenon, Belgian author of the Maigret novels, is an example of a Georges

explanation.surface: A typesetter crams a page with a Belgian crime novelist's work.
explanation.walkthrough: GEORGES has two Es; 'dropping earlier' removes the first, leaving GORGES.
explanation.definitionFit: To engorge is to swell by filling with blood or liquid, so it means fills to bursting.

clue.text: Less than half of Kansas backs booze for its capital

indicators.note: one piece backs another by coming behind it, so the Kansas letters follow the drink

parts.note: to tope is to drink heavily

indicators.note: only a third of the state name survives, the opening two of its six letters

explanation.surface: Only part of a state supports drinking, which seems to describe its capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Two of six letters is less than half, so the opening of the state's name follows the drink. 'Its' points back to Kansas, so the clue defines the city through the state.
explanation.definitionFit: Topeka is the seat of government of the US state named earlier in the clue.

clue.text: Audience's places in lounge

indicators.note: an audience hears rather than sees, so the word is taken as it sounds

parts.note: lays, as in lays down, means places

explanation.surface: A theatre audience's seats in the foyer bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lounge' looks like a noun but is the verb, to idle about.
explanation.definitionFit: To laze is to idle or loaf about, just as to lounge is.

clue.text: Turning off invention, sodium metal is coated with silver

indicators.note: the coating surrounds the core, so the silver letters go round the rest

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a lie is an invention or fabrication
Na is the chemical symbol for sodium
tin is a metal

explanation.surface: A dull chemistry lesson about plating a sodium compound with silver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is coated with' wraps silver's symbol round the other three pieces. 'Turning off' means repelling, not switching off.
explanation.definitionFit: Alienating someone means putting them off or estranging them, so it means repelling.

clue.text: Penetration, while I disapprove, stimulated sense

parts.note: as can mean while, as in 'as he spoke'
tut is the sound of disapproval

indicators.note: stimulated means stirred up, so the letters of sense are mixed

explanation.surface: Someone tutting as their senses are aroused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stimulated' rearranges SENSE to ENESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Penetration in the sense of keen insight or shrewdness, an ability to see through things.

clue.text: Inexperienced driver excluded from bar at all times

indicators.note: excluded means taken out, so one letter leaves the word for bar

parts.note: a lever is a bar used to prise or lift
L stands for learner, from the L-plate

explanation.surface: A learner driver turned away from a pub every time.
explanation.walkthrough: A British learner driver shows an L-plate, so L means learner; 'bar' is a crowbar, not a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Ever means always, forever.

clue.text: Men confounded with Greece's rise

indicators.note: confounded means confused or thrown together, so the letters are muddled

parts.note: the possessive adds no letter, leaving the country's name

explanation.surface: Men baffled by Greece's sudden ascent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confounded' mixes MEN + GREECE into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An emergence is a coming into view or rising up, as of a new power.

clue.text: Hollande's country makes a profit

definitions.meaning: the French word for a country, as François Hollande, former French president, would say
an enterprise that brings in returns is worthwhile

explanation.definitionFit: French pays means country or land; in English, a scheme that pays brings a financial return.

clue.text: Watch kick-off and middle of brutal hunt

parts.note: to see is to watch
KO is the usual abbreviation for kick-off in football fixtures

indicators.note: only the middle of the word is wanted, so its outer letters on each side are stripped away

explanation.surface: A football fan watching the start of a rough match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle of brutal' gives UT, the central pair of BRUTAL.
explanation.definitionFit: To seek out is to search for and find, as one does in a hunt.

clue.text: Prime slices of beef layered in crumbs then cooked by classy top chef

definitions.text: Prime slices of beef layered in crumbs then cooked
definitions.meaning: a dish of thin meat slices stuffed, layered, breaded and fried

explanation.walkthrough: 'By' just links the two definitions: the dish and the cook who might make it.
explanation.definitionFit: The French blue-ribbon phrase names a breaded stuffed escalope dish, and also a first-class cook.

clue.text: Saw through liquor run

parts.note: rum is a liquor
colours that run in the wash have bled

explanation.surface: A tale of drink flowing past, or a booze-run that was spotted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw through' is the verb to see through, to detect a deception.
explanation.definitionFit: Rumbled is British slang for found out or seen through a deception.

clue.text: Cause of illness of Usain Bolt unexpectedly leaving South Africa

indicators.note: unexpectedly suggests something turned out differently, so the remaining letters are rearranged
leaving means going out of, so letters for the country depart from the sprinter's name

explanation.surface: The sprinter fell ill on suddenly leaving South Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaving' removes SA from USAIN BOLT, leaving UINBOLT, which 'unexpectedly' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Botulin is the bacterial toxin responsible for botulism, a severe food poisoning.

clue.text: In recession, link records about moderate rate cap

indicators.note: recession means going back, so the whole assembled string is read backwards
about means surrounding, so one word goes round another

parts.note: a tie is a link or bond
mild means moderate
EPs are extended-play records

explanation.surface: An economic report: in a downturn, linking records to moderating a capped rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' puts the word for moderate inside the link; the records follow, and 'In recession' turns the whole string backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal maximum for road speed is a cap on the rate you may travel at.

clue.text: Academic place is up for second in Pop Idol

indicators.note: the replacement stands for the second letter in the word, swapping it out

parts.note: the word is used as printed

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: uni is short for university

explanation.surface: A university contestant on a TV talent show competing for second place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is up' turns UNI to INU, which replaces O, the second letter of POP. 'Pop Idol' was a British TV talent show, but here 'Idol' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A pin-up is someone admired whose picture is put on a wall, a heart-throb or idol.

clue.text: Gear regularly missing, though small

indicators.note: letters go missing at regular intervals, every other one

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as in clothing sizes

explanation.surface: Some kit keeps going missing, though it is small.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly missing' takes alternate letters of THOUGH: T, O, G.
explanation.definitionFit: Togs is informal British for clothes or kit.

clue.text: After financial source loses principal, a person is ruined

indicators.note: after signals that the second piece follows the first
the principal letter is the leading one, which goes

parts.note: a fund is a source of money
one means a person, as in 'one never knows'

explanation.surface: Someone ruined after a fund lost its capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Principal' looks financial (a capital sum) but means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Undone, as in 'I am undone', means ruined or brought to destruction.

clue.text: Cable connection covered by flannel and linen

indicators.note: the answer is covered by the fabric words, sitting inside them

explanation.surface: A cable wrapped in flannel and linen.
explanation.walkthrough: Look across 'flanneL AND LINEn'.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixed telephone line connected by physical cable, rather than mobile.

clue.text: Joint? Anorak contains more than half a dozen

indicators.note: contains means holds inside, so the rest goes within the other word

parts.note: a spod is a nerd or obsessive, like an anorak

indicators.note: four of the six letters of the number survive, more than half

parts.note: a dozen is twelve

explanation.surface: An anorak, the garment, with more than six items in it.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang an anorak is a nerd; 'more than half a dozen' trims TWELVE to TWEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A spot-weld is a join made by welding at a single point.

clue.text: Hospital uninvolved in intellectual mess

indicators.note: uninvolved means having no part in, so a letter is removed

parts.note: a thinker is an intellectual
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: A hospital having no part in an academic's muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mess' is the verb, as in to mess about with something.
explanation.definitionFit: To tinker is to fiddle or mess about with something.
